description: Breaking Ground talks from BSides Las Vegas 2022.

talks.title: Fragilience - The quantum state of survivable resilience in a world of fragile indifference
talks.teaser: Argues security should aim beyond resilience toward anti-fragility, using decision frameworks and team design.
talks.summary:
Chris Hoff opens by arguing that the security industry leans on words like resilience without defining them clearly. He draws on a regulator scenario where a bank was asked to assume all its controls had failed, and uses it to show how recovery targets and expectations can conflict. He also reviews anti-fragility, the idea that systems can get stronger from stress, and contrasts fragile, robust, resilient and anti-fragile responses.

The middle of the talk covers why he considers security more fragile than it should be. He points to a large number of sensors and tools without decision systems to act on their data, and surveys frameworks including the kill chain, ATT&CK, the NIST framework, threat modeling methods and quantitative risk models. He then introduces Cynefin's simple, complicated, complex and chaotic domains, safety science on human operators, and the reverse Conway's law, before walking through team topologies and how one company reorganized engineering teams around products. He also discusses the cybersecurity poverty line, the DevSecOps label applied without real change, and the punitive culture and militarized language that make security hard to work with.

He closes by urging practitioners to share lessons from incidents, organize teams around the services they deliver, and measure outcomes rather than only attacks stopped. The aim he sets is getting better from stressors, not just staying no worse than before. He presented the talk as a prompt for further discussion rather than a final answer.

talks.title: Watching the Watchers: Exploiting Vulnerable Monitoring Solutions
talks.teaser: Shows how trusted security appliances can become a point of compromise and how to limit the damage.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the premise that the security products an organization buys and trusts can be its weakest point. Such appliances often have broad access to email, workstations, servers and network traffic, so a compromise gives an attacker wide reach even when the initial flaw is a zero-day. The speakers argue that compliance standards are prescriptive, sometimes years out of date, and rarely account for a mandated security tool as the source of exposure. They recommend building tailored checklists based on the organization's own architecture and software.

Using the shift to remote work as an example, they describe how access paths added during the pandemic were poorly understood and how normal behavior drifted from the original baseline. Their suggested measures include just-enough administration in PowerShell, so administrators only get specific modules and commands, requiring signed scripts, and routing remote administration through controlled jump hosts instead of plain RDP. They also recommend rotating local administrator and service account passwords and Kerberos keys on a schedule, and using BloodHound to map trust relationships and likely attack paths. The talk closes with adversarial machine learning, where attackers can nudge malicious files past a classifier or flood analysts with false positives until alerts are ignored.

The final message is that trusted tools will eventually be abused, so defenders should assume failure and make changes in small, measured steps rather than rebuilding everything. The practical takeaways are to document what each privileged tool can reach, monitor deviations from that baseline, and involve administrators in every change.

talks.title: So You Wanta Build a C2?
talks.teaser: Covers what goes into building a command-and-control (C2) system.

talks.title: Scaling the Security Researcher to Eliminate OSS Vulnerabilities Once and For All
talks.teaser: Shows how bulk pull request generation with OpenRewrite and CodeQL can fix Java open source vulnerabilities at scale.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with an HTTP dependency-resolution flaw found in a Gradle build at the speaker's employer. Checking the wider Java ecosystem, he found the same weakness across many well-known organizations and repositories, and a coordinated push to move major artifact servers to HTTPS only still left many projects exposed. Filing issues by hand could not keep pace, so he set out to fix problems at scale instead.

The middle of the talk covers the tooling. CodeQL queries locate vulnerable projects, while OpenRewrite offers a format-preserving syntax tree for Java that lets recipes insert or rewrite code in each project's own style. The speakers walk through three Java flaws: temporary directory hijacking, partial path traversal and zip slip. For each, they explain why a naive fix can fall short, and how data flow and control flow analysis help confirm real issues and avoid false positives. They also describe GitHub API rate limits that slow bulk pull request creation.

The closing section gives practical lessons for anyone sending bulk fixes. Messages to maintainers should be careful, because maintainers are people. Commits should be signed off and GPG-signed, the effects of public disclosure should be weighed, and GitHub should be contacted in advance. The argument is that automated fixes can reach far more projects than individual reports, and listeners are pointed to OpenRewrite, CodeQL and open source security communities.

talks.title: See you later, allocator!': Updating Volatility's analysis of modern Linux memory allocators
talks.teaser: Shows how Volatility can carve kernel objects out of Linux's SLUB allocator to recover freed or hidden data.
talks.summary:
Memory forensics tools such as Volatility often rely on walking kernel linked lists to enumerate processes and network sockets. That approach misses anything the kernel has freed but not yet overwritten, and it becomes unreliable on modern Linux systems, where the SLUB allocator replaced the older SLAB design and no longer keeps complete lists of slabs. The talk explains how SLUB groups objects into size-based caches and tracks only partially allocated slabs, and why that breaks traditional enumeration.

The proposed method starts from a small kernel object that has already been located through other lists. From its address and the cache size, the plugin finds the enclosing slab and steps forward and backward through memory to extract every object in it, accepting that this produces a lot of noise. The work also updates an older slab-info plugin so it handles SLUB systems. In lab tests on virtual machines, carved sockets and processes were compared against netstat and ps output, and the method recovered objects the list-based plugins missed, including a process hidden by a BPFDoor-style rootkit.

The closing discussion covered the noise problem, whether a malware sample that scrubs itself from memory would still leave traces, and the limits of the technique for user-space content such as containers. Future work includes porting the plugin to Volatility 3 and filtering the output. The main takeaway for practitioners is that carving can recover freed or concealed kernel objects when list walking fails, and that newer kernel memory representations will change future Linux memory analysis.

talks.title: Injectyll-HIDe: Hardware Implants at Scale
talks.teaser: Presents open-source hardware implant tooling for recording keystrokes and networking many devices together.

talks.title: Putting Driver Signature Enforcement Tampering to Rest?!
talks.teaser: Shows new ways to bypass Windows driver signing enforcement by tampering with kernel memory, plus defenses against them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with background on driver signing enforcement, the Windows kernel feature that requires drivers to be signed before they load. It explains how the check is wired into the kernel through the ci.dll library and a callback structure, and how Microsoft's protections have grown over the years. Signing policies, a requirement for Microsoft to co-sign drivers, vulnerable-driver blocklists and the newer kernel data protection feature were each presented as steps that raise the cost of an attack.

The middle of the talk covers the common tampering approach, where an attacker locates an internal flag, overwrites it, loads a driver, and then restores the flag. The speaker then presented two new techniques. Page swapping redirects the virtual mapping for the flag's page to a writable copy by changing the physical frame number in the page table entries. Callback swapping instead redirects one of the validation callbacks to a function that already returns zero. Live demos on a recent Windows 11 build showed the older method triggering a blue screen under protection, while the new approaches let an unsigned test driver load.

The closing section proposed defenses. A defender could record the valid state at boot, watch for driver loading through registry or file system callbacks, and then restore or block any changes. The talk argued that virtualization-based protections such as HVCI are the most robust answer, though they remain uncommon in the field.

talks.title: Beyond logs and time series: observability for security & privacy
talks.teaser: Explains how observability tooling can answer security and privacy questions beyond traditional logs and time-series data.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from observability, a term that grew out of SRE circles, and contrasts it with traditional logging, alerting and time-series monitoring. Each approach slices system data differently: logs record past events as evidence, alerts fire on conditions defined in advance, metrics capture state over time, and tracing follows a request across services. Combined, these let teams query a running system rather than reconstruct incidents by hand.

For security work, the main gain is the ability to pivot and join across data on the fly. An investigator can start from one suspicious session, check whether a credential was used elsewhere, or narrow scope by geography or subsystem. Operational and security teams often query the same data for different questions, so shared tooling can serve both if it is adapted. The speaker also covered benefits such as better alignment between development, operations and security, automation, behavioral alerting, and easier audit evidence. The costs include dynamic tracing that attackers can misuse, a false sense of completeness from single-pane dashboards, and weak support for legacy systems.

On privacy, opaque identifiers let traces follow data through a system without exposing the underlying values. The closing advice was to test vendor claims by running red-team activity against candidate tools, to treat access to observability capabilities like root access, and to decide deliberately what gets monitored and learn from each incident. The question period touched on query workflows, federating data sources, and checking whether a compromised collection agent can be caught by comparing its output with independent sensors.

talks.title: A Tale of Two Malware Families - Overcoming Anti-Forensics and Foiling Botnets in the Cloud
talks.teaser: Dissects two cloud malware families that use time stomping and renamed binaries to evade forensics and detection.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with what the speaker calls the cloud challenge: attackers keep moving toward cloud compute, containers and serverless services, while defenders often lack visibility into their environments. Although most cloud intruders rely on simple shell scripts rather than advanced exploits, they use Linux-specific tricks to slow down investigators.

The first family, CoinStomp, is a cryptojacking campaign aimed mainly at Asian cloud providers. The researchers described how it copies chmod and chattr to new names and uses touch with hard-coded dates to rewrite timestamps, and how it attempts to remove system cryptographic policies. It also opens a plain-text reverse shell over port 443, uses a cron job to kill tail and mask, and references an older campaign to muddy attribution. Their test showed that file creation times still exposed the tampering. The second family, ABC Bot, spreads through initialization scripts, removes rival miners, disables cloud security agents, plants SSH keys and propagates via known hosts. Comparing it with the Xanthi campaign revealed shared function layout, identical usernames and a common command-and-control address in iptables rules, suggesting one actor behind both.

The talk closes with a recent Watchdog example that hid processes by filtering renamed ps output through grep and used a directory named with an ellipsis to mimic the parent directory. Practical advice includes auditing hosts, avoiding exposed Docker and Redis services, watching /usr/bin and /bin for renamed binaries, keeping a vaccine host with known hosts entries, enabling cloud logging, and alerting on touch with time-setting flags.

talks.title: Everything I know about prototype pollutions: how to react when confronted to a brand new vuln
talks.teaser: Traces how prototype pollution was found and handled in npm, from a bug bounty report to real-world Node.js exploits.
talks.summary:
The talk follows the history of prototype pollution in the JavaScript ecosystem, starting with a 2018 bug bounty report that affected a dozen npm packages. The speaker, who ran the Node.js ecosystem bounty program at the time, describes how the team first had to decide whether the issue was a real security flaw or only a code quality defect. Before reaching the exploit, the talk explains how JavaScript objects inherit properties through their prototype chain, using a debugger to show where inherited methods come from.

From there, the talk shows how a recursive merge function can be tricked into writing to the global prototype, so every object in a process picks up attacker-chosen properties. It covers a similar path in lodash through the constructor, then two real cases: a denial of service caused by replacing a method with a string, and a remote code execution in Kibana where a polluted environment variable was inherited by a child process. A later issue in a MongoDB-backed API service, which chained the pollution into a deserialization option, is also described.

For defense, the speaker recommends rejecting proto and constructor keys from untrusted input, validating object shapes with schemas, creating prototype-less objects, and disabling proto where possible. The closing reflections are that the team should have involved Node.js core earlier to model the threat, and that static analysis still struggled with this bug class.

talks.title: Lateral Movement and other Creative Steps Attackers Take in AWS
talks.teaser: Maps how attackers move between AWS accounts and VPCs via roles, peering and IAM privilege escalation, with detection ideas.
talks.summary:
The talk starts by contrasting cloud and on-premises networks. In AWS, workloads sit in the data plane while the API-driven control plane manages resources, and an attacker often has to cross both. Classic on-prem tactics such as ARP discovery do not work inside VPCs, so the speaker describes alternatives: scanning address ranges, pivoting from a compromised instance through its attached role, and using stolen keys to call APIs directly.

The middle section covers movement between accounts. Trust policies that let one account assume a role in another can be chained, and the speaker shows how bouncing between control-plane role assumptions and data-plane instances can get around session limits. Account IDs and role names, often guessable or exposed in logs and policies, make this easier. The talk also reviews IAM privilege escalation techniques, noting that they differ in how quickly they reach administrator access, and points to a policy analysis tool for finding them. Common designs such as hub-and-spoke networking, shared CI/CD accounts and an AWS Organizations management account are presented as risky.

To close, the speaker presents a prototype graph tool that loads account and resource data into a graph database and visualises likely lateral movement and escalation paths, demonstrated on mock-up client data. Practical takeaways include applying least privilege with permission boundaries and service control policies, keeping the management account empty, reviewing cross-account trust, and segmenting accounts and networks.

talks.title: Cookie Monster: Exfiltrating Data and More, Byte by Tasty Byte
talks.teaser: Shows how a red team hid stolen data inside ordinary web cookies to slip past inspection proxies and DLP controls.
talks.summary:
Two security consultants describe a 2018 red team engagement in which the client allowed only HTTPS outbound, routed traffic through an inspection proxy, and ran data loss prevention. The team needed a quick, low-tech way to move a file of sensitive records off the network without drawing attention. They chose ordinary web cookies as the hiding place, since cookie traffic is everywhere and rarely scrutinized in detail.

The first prototype, built in Node behind Apache for TLS, used a PowerShell feeder that encoded the file, split it into chunks, and sent them as cookie values over normal GET requests with a spoofed user agent and randomized delays. A server reassembled the data. It evaded the controls, but the odd formatting would stand out to anyone reading closely. The second version added device identifiers, padding, retries for lost chunks, a web interface, configurable headers and cookie sizes, and a heartbeat that polls the server for a single command. The live demo showed a file arriving intact while the proxy saw what looked like routine browsing.

The presenters were candid about limits. Transfers need many requests, encoding inflates file size, and a fresh destination can be caught by reputation filtering. Cookies sent before any server set them could also trigger false positives. Defenders were pointed toward behavioral baselines: what normally talks to where, and which destinations or traffic patterns are new. They invited others to test the tool, since it had not yet been proven against a monitored network.

talks.title: Detecting Log4J on a global scale using collaborative security
talks.teaser: Shows how a shared, community-fed blocklist helped detect and block Log4j exploitation across the globe.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces CrowdSec, a free and open-source agent that uses rule-based scenarios to detect attacks on a server and sends the offending IPs to a central consensus engine. The engine publishes a shared blocklist back to every participating agent. The speaker explains how the network resists poisoning through trust ranks that grow over months, per-network voting that limits any one actor's influence, and comparison against the project's own honeypots. A whitelist of common services such as search engine crawlers and CDNs guards against false positives. Privacy is kept narrow: only the source IP, a timestamp and the scenario name are shared.

The main case study is Log4j. CrowdSec published a detection scenario within a day of the December 2021 disclosure and revised it several times as attackers obfuscated their payloads, eventually reaching 34 matching patterns and Unicode support. Community signals quickly identified around a thousand actively exploiting IPs. One scanner turned out to be a German research institute, and the team chose not to block it. Later spikes were less clear, though one was loosely linked to a US government warning about a VMware Horizon flaw. In a controlled experiment with two identical servers, 92 percent of hostile traffic to the protected server was blocked using community reputation alone.

The talk also covered SSH and SIP brute forcing, a layer 7 denial-of-service wave, and how quickly hosting providers cleaned up compromised machines, with averages differing widely between providers. The practical takeaway is that no single control should be relied on, and shared reputation data can close the gap before a local detector sees an attack.

talks.title: Ransomware Emulation Done Right
talks.teaser: Shows how a large company ran a controlled ransomware simulation and what its purple-team exercises revealed about detection gaps.
talks.summary:
The speakers from eBay open by arguing that ransomware is costly enough to justify testing defenses before an attack. Their program asks three questions: whether employees are susceptible, whether controls and tools actually work, and whether the response is the right one. Education and phishing awareness sit in one track, while purple-team exercises and red-team work cover the controls side. They also describe a sandboxing workflow in which ransomware samples from public repositories run in an isolated cloud virtual machine so the team can see whether endpoint tooling blocks or detects them.

Early testing with a custom payload written in C# and Go was caught by endpoint canary files, which the speakers then bypassed by skipping files with certain name prefixes and by injecting into a trusted process. The exercise produced detection rules for Windows Defender tampering, process injection, and misuse of certutil, and it exposed logging gaps such as missing process command lines, which strengthened the case for a Sysmon rollout. A live simulation followed, limited to directors and above, with executive approval and a short time window. It surfaced problems with help desk handling and the advice to shut down machines instead of isolating them, and the after-action interviews with staff added useful detail.

The talk closes with an intel-driven response to a Microsoft Office URL handler flaw, where detections were built within 48 hours and a workaround was deployed to more than 15,000 hosts after red-team validation. The main takeaways are that red and blue collaboration speeds up detection work, that sandboxing is a low-cost way to check tooling, and that simulations need leadership sign-off and careful planning. The speakers left the question of paying a ransom to legal and executive leadership.

talks.title: CLOSING
talks.teaser: Closes the event with thanks to staff, volunteers and players, plus auction results and pool party details.
talks.summary:
The closing session opens with thanks to the people behind the Prose vs. Joe's capture-the-flag game, which runs live ranges with blue teams defending systems while red teams attack them. The organizer describes how players and captains prepare for weeks, how the red team acts more as an educator than an aggressor, and how a remote gold team watched systems and kept the game running. The organizer also says it was their first time running the game.

Next comes a silent auction update, which raised over 2,000 dollars from more than 35 items, many donated by sponsors and attendees. The director then describes the first in-person year since 2019, with a smaller crowd than before by design and roughly 1,600 badges covered by donations. New staff and volunteers stepped in on short notice, and individual staff members are recognized for logistics, web, graphic design, sponsor operations and speaker operations. Remote helpers who could not attend in person are also thanked. A longtime figure in the BSides movement, who was absent this year, is remembered.

The session closes with plans to hold the next event at the same Las Vegas venue, with dates to follow once DEF CON confirms its schedule. Attendees are invited to send feedback by email or social messages, since formal surveys are not run. The closing reminds the audience of the pool party and thanks sponsors, donors, the board, speakers and attendees for making the event possible.
